_why: Terms shown with a hover card (see glossary-plugin.ts) and listed on /glossary. Each definition is a paraphrase of the official docs: 'source' is the upstream/ chapter and 'phrase' a sentence fragment from it that must still be there (scripts/audit.py checks). 'match' are the words that get the card (first one on a page, in running text only). 'in' limits a term to pages whose path starts with one of these, for words that are also ordinary English.

terms.definition: Elixir's unit of concurrency: code always runs inside one. Processes are isolated, run concurrently and talk by passing messages. They are not operating system processes, and are lightweight enough to run in the hundreds of thousands.
terms.phrase: Processes are isolated from each other, run concurrent to one another and communicate via message passing

terms.definition: A process identifier. It is what `spawn/1` returns and what `send/2` takes to reach that process.
terms.phrase: PID

terms.definition: Where the messages sent to a process wait. `receive/1` searches it for a message that matches a pattern. Sending does not block: the sender puts the message in the mailbox and carries on.
terms.phrase: the message is stored in the process mailbox

terms.definition: A relationship between two processes for the case of failure: if one fails, the other receives an exit signal. Without a link, a failure in one process never crashes another.
terms.phrase: If we want the failure in one process to propagate to another one, we should link them

terms.definition: A one-way way to track when a process dies, without tying exit signals together. When the monitored process ends, the watcher gets a message, whatever the reason.
terms.phrase: If we simply want to track when a process dies, without tying their exit signals to each other, a better solution is to use monitors

terms.definition: The message a process sends along its links when it ends. A linked process that isn't trapping exits ends too, unless the reason is `:normal`.
terms.phrase: EXIT signal

terms.definition: Setting `Process.flag(:trap_exit, true)` so exit signals arrive as ordinary messages instead of ending the process. Supervisors do this to survive their children.
terms.phrase: supervisors trap exits from links

terms.definition: A process that detects when its children die and starts new ones in their place. Processes are often linked to a supervisor for this.
terms.phrase: supervisors which will detect when a process dies and start a new process in its place

terms.definition: Supervisors whose children can be supervisors themselves, so the processes of an application form a tree.
terms.phrase: giving us supervision trees

terms.definition: A map that tells a supervisor how to start, shut down and restart one child. It is usually written as `{module, options}` or just the module name.
terms.phrase: The child specification describes how the supervisor starts, shuts down,

terms.definition: A "generic server": a process that holds state and offers synchronous (call) and asynchronous (cast) requests, plus code reloading and more.
terms.phrase: "Generic servers" (processes) that encapsulate state

terms.definition: A simple wrapper around state: a process you read and update by passing functions.
terms.phrase: Simple wrappers around state

terms.definition: An asynchronous computation: spawn it now and read its result later.
terms.phrase: Asynchronous units of computation that allow spawning a process

terms.definition: Open Telecom Platform: the set of libraries that ships with Erlang, used to build robust, fault-tolerant applications. It includes supervision trees and event managers.
terms.phrase: is a set of libraries that ships with Erlang

terms.definition: Every Elixir project is an application, and so is Elixir itself (`:elixir`) and parts of it such as `:ex_unit`.
terms.phrase: Every Elixir project is an application

terms.definition: A running Erlang VM that can connect to others. Processes are location transparent: sending a message works the same whether the recipient is on this node or another.
terms.phrase: location transparent

terms.definition: Erlang Term Storage: the `:ets` and `:dets` modules store large data structures in memory or on disk.
terms.phrase: Erlang Term Storage (ETS)

terms.definition: Abstract Syntax Tree. Elixir represents code as nested tuples shaped like a tree, and calls them quoted expressions.
terms.phrase: Abstract Syntax Tree

terms.definition: Elixir's name for the AST: code represented as nested tuples, which `quote` produces and `unquote` splices into.
terms.phrase: Elixir calls them *quoted expressions*

terms.definition: Code that receives quoted expressions and transforms them into something else. Macros are harder to write than functions, and it is bad style to use them when they aren't needed.
terms.phrase: receiving quoted expressions and transforming them into something else

terms.definition: Macros have "late resolution": a variable defined inside a `quote` won't conflict with one in the code where the macro is expanded.
terms.phrase: a variable defined inside a quote won't conflict

terms.definition: A custom textual representation. It starts with `~`, then a letter and a delimiter, with optional modifiers after the last delimiter. You can define your own.
terms.phrase: Sigils start with the tilde

terms.definition: A list of code points, written `~c"like this"`, mostly used for interoperability with Erlang.
terms.phrase: which are often used for interoperability with Erlang

terms.definition: A bitstring whose number of bits is divisible by 8. Every binary is a bitstring, but not every bitstring is a binary.
terms.phrase: A binary is a bitstring where the number of bits is divisible by 8

terms.definition: A mechanism for polymorphism: behaviour varies with the data type, dispatching on the type of the first argument. Anyone can implement a protocol, at any time.
terms.phrase: dispatching will always be based on the data type of the first input

terms.definition: An extra condition on a clause, written after `when`. A clause only matches if the pattern matches and the guard is true.
terms.phrase: Clauses also allow extra conditions to be specified via guards

terms.definition: An example in a documentation string, written with an `iex>` prompt and the expected result on the next line, checked as a test so documentation stays accurate.
terms.phrase: Doctests are specified by an indentation of four spaces followed by the

terms.definition: An extension built on top of maps that adds compile-time checks and default values.
terms.phrase: Structs are extensions built on top of maps that provide compile-time checks and default values

terms.definition: `|>` takes the result of the expression on its left and passes it as the first argument of the call on its right, to highlight the data being transformed.
terms.phrase: passes it as the first argument to the function call on its right side

terms.definition: Syntactic sugar for looping over an enumerable, filtering and mapping, grouped into the `for` special form.
terms.phrase: Comprehensions are syntactic sugar

terms.definition: A list of two-element tuples whose first element, the key, is an atom. Keys keep the order you gave and can repeat. Mostly used for optional arguments to functions.
terms.phrase: they are lists consisting of 2-item tuples where the first element (the key) is an atom

terms.definition: A fixed collection written with curly brackets that can hold any value. Its elements are stored contiguously in memory, so reading one by index or getting the size is fast.
terms.phrase: Tuples store elements contiguously in memory

terms.definition: A constant whose value is its own name, such as `:ok`. Two atoms are equal if their names are equal.
terms.phrase: An atom is a constant whose value is its own name

terms.definition: The `=` operator is the match operator. Besides matching simple values, it destructures complex data such as tuples, binding variables to the parts.
terms.phrase: The match operator is not only used to match against simple values, but it is also useful for destructuring more complex data types

terms.definition: Data structures are never changed in place: operations return new ones. You can pass data around knowing no one will mutate it in memory, only transform it.
terms.phrase: One advantage of immutability is that it leads to clearer code

terms.definition: A function your module defines that a process behaviour calls under specific conditions, such as `init/1` or `handle_call/3` for a GenServer.
terms.phrase: A GenServer is a process that invokes a limited set of functions under specific conditions

terms.definition: A module such as `GenServer` or `Supervisor` that defines the callbacks your module implements so it can run as that kind of process. Your module declares it with `@behaviour`, or with `use`.
terms.phrase: A behaviour module for implementing supervisors
